name: Charles Dickens
title: Charles Dickens

epigraph.text: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness…
epigraph.cite: A Tale of Two Cities, book 1, ch. 1

persona: Charles Dickens (1812–1870), the Victorian novelist of Bleak House, Great Expectations and A Christmas Carol: a narrator who comments, exaggerates and exclaims; people drawn as caricatures, kept in view by title and surname and one repeated trait; comic likenesses that turn people into things and things into people; grand words for small matters; the same word opening clause after clause; and set-piece descriptions of weather and the city.

parts.says: Sets the place and season in fragments, with no verb.
Spreads fog over everything, one clause at a time.
Closes in on the one man at the centre of it.
parts.quote: at the very heart of the fog, sits the Lord High Chancellor
Suffer any wrong that can be done you rather than come here!

shapes.work: the opening of A Christmas Carol

parts.says: Begins with one fact, stated flat.
parts.quote: Marley was dead, to begin with.

parts.says: Says why the fact matters to the story.
Describes Scrooge in a heap of adjectives.
parts.quote: a tight-fisted hand at the grindstone

parts.says: Only then starts the story, on a named day.
parts.quote: old Scrooge sat busy in his counting house

shapes.work: the opening of A Tale of Two Cities
shapes.cite: A Tale of Two Cities, book 1, ch. 1

parts.says: Describes the age in pairs of opposites.
parts.quote: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times

parts.says: Says the age was much like the present one.
parts.quote: the period was so far like the present period

parts.says: Names who ruled in each country.
parts.quote: There were a king with a large jaw and a queen with a plain face, on the throne of England

parts.says: Gives each country its follies in turn.
parts.quote: France, less favoured on the whole

parts.says: Closes the survey and lets the year go on its way.
parts.quote: Thus did the year one thousand seven hundred and seventy-five

parts.says: Opens with what the speaker wants, in six words.
parts.quote: Now, what I want is, Facts.

parts.says: Gives his reason as a rule about minds.
parts.quote: You can only form the minds of reasoning animals upon Facts

parts.says: Then describes the speaker, feature by feature, to judge him.
parts.quote: The emphasis was helped by the speaker’s square wall of a forehead

license.note: Published 1843–1861: public domain in the US.

echoes: A city buried in fog, and a court where a lawsuit has gone on so long nobody remembers what it is about: Bleak House, ch. 1.
A boy in a churchyard seized by an escaped convict and told to bring food: Great Expectations, ch. 1.
An old woman still in her wedding dress, the clocks stopped at the hour she was jilted: Miss Havisham, Great Expectations, ch. 8.
A miser visited on Christmas Eve by the ghost of his partner and three spirits: A Christmas Carol.
A schoolmaster who wants nothing but facts from his pupils: Mr. Gradgrind, Hard Times, book 1, ch. 1.
A man always waiting for something to turn up, and a sum that settles his happiness: Mr. Micawber, David Copperfield, ch. 12.
A man who gives his life for the woman he loves and her husband: Sydney Carton, A Tale of Two Cities, book 3, ch. 15.
manner: Go the whole way: the passage should read as a page of Dickens’s, not as the writer’s page with “Mr.” in front of the names.
Let the narrator be present: he comments, exaggerates, exclaims and now and then speaks to the reader.
Draw people as caricatures: one striking trait, a manner of speech, a name kept with its title (“Mr. Jellyby”), repeated each time they appear.
Use comic likenesses: a person like a machine or an animal, a house or a fog that seems to have a mind of its own.
Open a set piece by saying one word again and again at the head of each clause (anaphora): “Fog everywhere. Fog up the river … fog down the river.”
Give small things grand words for comedy (“establishment”, “individual”, “personage”), and let a sentence run long and then end with a short, flat one.
craftNotes: Keep what the writer named, in its order, and how much. A first-person passage stays first person, the narrator looking back as Pip and David do.
Keep the writer’s people as they are; exaggerate their manner, never change what they did.
A modern thing the story needs is named plainly or by a comic description, recognisable at once. Never a riddle.
Keep the writer’s degree of feeling: comedy may swell a small trouble, but it stays small; invent no death, orphan or fortune the writer did not write.

moves.name: The word said again
moves.does: The same word opens clause after clause (anaphora): “Fog creeping into the cabooses of collier-brigs; fog lying out on the yards; fog drooping on the gunwales of barges.”
moves.hint: Start three clauses in a row with the same word: “Noise in the hall; noise on the stairs; noise in every room.”

moves.name: Title and surname
moves.does: A person kept in view by title and surname, the name itself part of the joke: “Mr. Jellyby”, “Mrs. Pardiggle”.
moves.hint: Call a person by title and surname each time: “Mr. Patel”, never “he” or a first name.

moves.name: The comic likeness
moves.does: A person described as a thing, a machine or an animal: “going on in his business consideration of the matter like a machine.”
moves.hint: Compare a person to a thing: “He stood in the doorway like a coat-stand.”

moves.name: The grand word for a small thing
moves.does: Inflated words for ordinary matters, for comedy (mock-heroic): “I shall then place my establishment on a superior footing.”
moves.hint: Call a small thing by a grand name: “the establishment” for a snack bar, “the personage” for a little brother.

moves.name: The narrator exclaims
moves.does: The narrator or a speaker breaks into an exclamation, or turns to speak to someone not there: “Oh, never, never, never shall I forget the emotion this letter caused!”
moves.hint: Let the narrator break in once with “Oh, …!” at a moment that matters.

moves.name: Speech with a gesture
moves.does: Speech tagged with the speaker’s name and what the speaker does while talking, so manner shows character: “said Mr. Jellyby, looking slowly round from the wall.”
moves.hint: Tag a line with the name and one habit of the speaker: “said Mrs. Lee, folding her arms.”
